In your previous testimony, I found something interesting about this document, where you say that the document is not addressed to any of the sectors. Do you see that also in this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not addressed to any unit or sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And should it have been addressed to anyone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order -- or an instruction, I can't tell. Perhaps it's in the text. Something that should be implemented by subordinate units. Perhaps it's contained at the bottom of the page, but it refers to all the units, the intelligence security units and organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, if we could go to the last page to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we can see that this is signed by General Ratko Mladic. In the original, on the left-hand side, do you recognise General Mladic's signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here "for." It does say "Commander, Colonel General Ratko Mladic," but by hand, it's written "za," "for," and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this is not General Mladic's signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would now need to look at the first page again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if I can help, it says here in the last sentence: "Forward these instructions and inform of their content all commanders of units and institutions down to battalion level." Meaning down to the regiments and brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I do agree that this is not General Mladic's signature. And there -- you may recall we have heard evidence from a VRS officer who this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think this is Zdravko Tolimir's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document does contain the type of work that General Tolimir was doing.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does refer to the work of the organs that he led.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the first page of the document now, please. Can we look at this part of the heading with the numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the number that the document is registered under?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 18. That number, I think, refers to the log-book of the intelligence security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you something about the time when you went to Jasenica. That is the western part of the front; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were there, did you receive combat reports from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about that in my previous testimony. Those reports that were written to the Supreme Command and to the corps were sent to the Main Staff forward command post or posts, if there were several of them. So they would be sent to one or to all of them, if there were more than one. I think this is also in the heading of some reports that Mr. McCloskey showed to me yesterday, that the IKM of the Main Staff is also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who signed the regular combat reports?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The block signature would be the Chief of the Main Staff, General Milovanovic. After a certain period of time, the signature would say, "Representing the Chief of Staff, Major-General Radivoje Miletic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we were using the word "zastupa" which has normally been translated into "standing in" and it's a slightly different terminology, I believe, in the VRS. Just, Mr. Lukic, may be able to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you, in your questions, I think, "standing in" and "for" or "standing in for" was one of your favourite subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you check whether there's any chance that your question may have been misunderstood by the witness or ... or by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It would also be helpful for the interpreters to have one of these documents because then they will see the CLSS translation. Because somehow "representing" got in there, and I think we should try to be consistent on this if it's going to be something --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not going again to ask about "standing in" but about the period of time when the signature of General Milovanovic appeared on those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. That's fine. Mr. McCloskey has some concern about an inconsistency on a -- very much a detail of the language used in documents. Could you, perhaps even together with CLSS, make a short agenda saying, If this appears, the proper translation is that, if that appears, so that we don't have to go through all of the translations of all of the documents if there possibly are any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, and like many things here, this has been done before and, as I'm sure the Defence will agree, General Milovanovic was in the Krajina for many, many days in 1995, and he has gone through all those reports and identified all the times that he was gone and all the times that it says "standing in." And that's what you're talking about. General Milovanovic will be here. But the term "representing," when that gets thrown into the mix, that complicates things. That's my only objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two ways, Mr. McCloskey. Either we ask for a formal verification of translation or you have pointed at a term which is unfamiliar to you, knowing a lot of these documents. One of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The translations are fine. It just -- I think caught the booth off guard. If they'd seen the actual translation, they would have been fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let me -- let me see. When I said "verification of the translation," I should have said "verification of the interpretation." Do you seek that or do you think that you have sufficiently drawn our attention to this matter? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't want to try to control the booth. I think they do a great job, but I just I know this "representation" word is problematic and perhaps they'll think about it and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we hear from the booth. I think we all share our admiration and appreciation for the great work done. Is there any chance that "represented" would be better translated by - and now I hope not to make any mistake - "standing in"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, "zastupati" does translate into English as "standing in for."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it would happen that in the signature it would say that a report was signed by General Milovanovic, even though, at the same time, he was with you in the western sector of the front.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's obvious that he could not have signed that, but that somebody signed that in his name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the document that would come under encryption does not contain a signature. It would just contain a typed signature. Mr. McCloskey knows that in one proceedings here I talked about General Miletic and how this came about. And if you like, I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you about that briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am going to object now and if he does have a -- such a document, he should show it to the witness because my recollection is all those documents say "standing in for the commander" -- or, sorry, "standing in for the Chief of Staff." And so it's very clear, it's not one of these documents that is under the name of the person and it's not clear because it's a teletype.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you commenting on the answer of the witness or are you objecting to a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm objecting. He is suggesting something that I do not believe is reflected in the evidence. If he has an example of that, he should show it. My recollection is the documents that are going to the president, they say: General Miletic standing in for the Chief of Staff. There may be some that are Milovanovic, that you can't tell, but I don't think so and I'd like to see them if they are before he puts that in a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exactly. Could you give line -- we're on page 53. Where exactly it is, Mr. McCloskey, that you're objecting to? Page and line number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I see on page 52, starting line 14: "Well, it's obvious that he could not have signed that but that somebody signed that in his name; is that correct?" And then also above that, line 10: "So it would happen that in a signature it would say that a report was signed by General Milovanovic even though, at the same time, he was with you ..." My point is, it does not say that it was signed by Milovanovic. It says, it's my recollection, Miletic standing in for Milovanovic. That may be the point Mr. Lukic is trying to get across, but I don't want to leave the impression that he's leaving in that question because it's not correct. And I go back to my original point, if we just put a document up there that he is referring to, it would all be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I don't have the document. I -- I don't have it, the number, so I can call it but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The basis of my question was 65 ter number 29091, uploaded by the Prosecution as the witness statement of this witness. And it -- in e-court, page 27, we can find the same -- almost the same words uttered by this gentleman. So if we go to 65 ter 29091, e-court page 27, which corresponds to page 28233 from the 14th of November, 2008, testimony in Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Lines 10 to 16. I will read. "Q. In that part of the front line in the forward command post in question, from Manojlo Milovanovic was there from the end of October, wasn't he? Do you know whose signatures did combat reports bear? "A. Since it was an encrypted communication, in the bottom left part of each telegram, there was the so-called block signature featuring the chief of General Staff, Colonel General Manojlo Milovanovic, but we doubt his actual signature." So that was the base of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The inference in the question was that it was not clear from the document who was signing when it in fact is from the document. You can see it says "standing in for."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Lukic, having heard all the problems raised by Mr. McCloskey, is there any way that you could rephrase your question in such a way that you get the answer you're seeking, and, at the same time, that Mr. McCloskey doesn't further object?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can withdraw the question. It is nothing crucial for us at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The question is withdrawn. We leave it to that .

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's another point you should be familiar with as Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a matter for re-examination Mr. McCloskey or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I think it helps clear up why I'm concerned with this point. And it shouldn't be anything that could cause the witness a problem and it's short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very short, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have seen Bratunac Brigade reports that are typed sign under the name of Vidoje Blagojevic, when Vidoje Blagojevic was at Zepa and they brought that out very clearly and that's a fair point and that was part of what they wanted to get across that we don't contest. This is not that situation, and I don't want you to be confused and think it is. Because it's a very different document with very different communications but they're making it sound like it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you would keep it short. I think to the extent you would show further any documents to the witness, you can do so in re-examination and we should not yet end up in argument at this moment. Mr. Lukic, question withdrawn, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With one remark that we'll try to find the document with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm certain that Mr. McCloskey will appreciate that. And so will the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. May I proceed, Your Honour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't bother you with this anymore, but we are still at the forward command post on the western front, and you're still there with General Milovanovic. Is it true that General Milovanovic, while he was staying at the forward command post, had all -- all necessary means of communication available?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At forward command posts, all types of communications are set up that also exist at the basic command post, only to a lesser extent. There are communications lines going to the superior command, to the subordinates, and the basic command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does TKT stand for? Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Confidential commanding of troops. It's an abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are TKT documents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're documents that are compiled and through which command is carried out in order to protect the confidentiality of documents. Operatives do that. It's part of cryptographic protection. Keys are changed often so the one listening in on our communications would have to have the required key to know what the communication was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now to set up a link with this topic, is it true that for someone to be able to exercise command, he would have to have both a means of communication and a TKT?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from regular combat reports, General Milovanovic also received oral reports from the VRS Main Staff. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't with him all the time, but communication lines were available. Since I was staying at the command post most of the time, if General Milovanovic was delayed, I would receive calls from the Main Staff and speak about the situation in the area. To what extent he communicated and with whom, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate, General Milovanovic, had he not had these means of communication or those TKT documents, he wouldn't have been able to follow the situation in the theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have been able to the same extent as corps commands. Because the reports from the Main Staff that we drafted for the Supreme Command were also sent to corps commands and to forward command posts of the Main Staff. So if a report goes to the Supreme Command, the one at the forward command post of the Main Staff will also get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So they would only be in a position to receive written reports.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter, from the Prosecutor's list, 25931, please. It's a short document. It should be possible to display it on one screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be enlarged a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see it? Please read it. No, you don't have to read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the second page in English so we see the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go back in English version to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see that the Herzegovina Corps Command, on the 1st of August, 1995, sent a communication from its forward command post number 1. It is very urgent. And to whom do they send their communication?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says to the Main Staff of the VRS, then the 2nd Krajina Corps, and to General Mladic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to this document, where was General Mladic located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Command of the Herzegovina Corps has information that General Mladic was staying with the 2nd Krajina Corps. That's why this was sent to the Main Staff; more specifically, the 2nd Krajina Corps, and General Mladic personally who was there. So they know where he was. They are requesting that the neighbouring corps - and that's the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps - take over the features taken because it's in the zone of responsibility of the latter corps anyway. But since the Herzegovina Corps cannot command the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, they are turning to General Mladic to order the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to do what's required here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm closing to an end. So maybe we could make a break now and I can reorganise my questions, and I will probably have a couple of more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Couple of more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break first. We'll first have the witness escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we resume at 1.30. Half past 1.00. Mr. McCloskey, is the next witness ready to start the examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have to check. I'm not sure. I won't have too much ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, Janet tells me they are ready. And I don't have too much re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then prepare for every possible way of proceeding. We'll take the break and resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we're wrapping up. Before I continue with you, I'll have to address the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender 1D1100. That's a decision from the Official Gazette about the establishment of a state committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just one second. No objections, Mr. McCloskey. I apologise for being -- my attention was drawn in a different direction for a second. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1100 receives number D336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And another document we used today, 65 ter 14596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You tender that as well? Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14596 receives number D337, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D337 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. This is done now. Could we please see 65 ter 25569.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will see, General, that it's an agreement on the disarmament of able-bodied persons in the Zepa enclave. Did you know at the time that this agreement had been reached?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the agreement, but I didn't see it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the preamble, preceding para 1, we read that on the 25th of July, 1995, the following agreement was reached between Rajko Kusic on one side and Hamdija Kolak from the other side. It says "Kolak" but I believe it should be "Torlak" instead. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Torlak is more likely, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I clipped a part of this document from another version, but never mind that. In the presence of Sejmon Dudnjik as UNPROFOR's representative. You knew that the Ukrainian battalion was in Zepa, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we could agree that that is Hamdija Torlak, it should be. That this is a typo or a mistake of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Dudnjik was the commander of this Ukrainian battalion at Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After this agreement was reached, civilians started leaving Zepa; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask a few questions to start with. I point some matters which my attention is drawn to. The document starts by saying: "Today, the 25th of July, 1995 ..." At the very end of the document, it says: "24th of July, 1995, 18.30 hours." Paragraph 11 of the agreement says: "The agreement shall come into the effect immediately after signing." I looked in e-court, and I did not find either of the versions, English or B/C/S, to be signed. So that these are a few matters before we start asking about ... I've got no idea what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the English signature block, we see now the right name Torlak, as agreed by the parties. But the first name is different from here. It is Hakija instead of Hamdija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So these are five preliminary questions apart from that Mr. Mladic is also someone at the bottom mentioned as someone apparently expected to sign this document. These are all the -- we are lawyers, Mr. Lukic, so, therefore, I would like to draw your attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Actually, I have completely different cutout from the same, allegedly the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This apparently what was uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. We'll try probably to replace it, then, because I have D51 from Tolimir case and it's completely -- completely different document, completely differently typed. So we'll probably see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have that cutout so I don't see it. And I don't have that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- because it's under different number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps to clarify, D51 seems to be the number from Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From Tolimir case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's proceed, but please keep in the back of your mind that all these questions are still without an answer for the Chamber, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I used 65 ter number. Maybe it was more wise for me to upload, but it is obviously too late now. We'll do it probably in a couple of days and try to use with somebody else. But I think that even without the document, I can pose a couple of more questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do have a signed document. Though that doesn't resolve other issues with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With Hakija and Hamdija?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I was thinking of whether it was an agreement or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, please -- the text of the document is the same, more or less, Mr. McCloskey, then we can continue. And we are now informed that, most likely, a signed copy can be produced. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask, nevertheless, Mr. McCloskey, four signatures?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart is nodding yes so I would not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: More reliable source, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can, of course, print one out right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- if you could do that, then we could have a look at it. Could we ... let's proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just receiving information from General Mladic that he thinks that he did not sign this document but we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look at the printed-out version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true, General, that after the departure of civilians from Zepa, armed Muslim units at Zepa failed to act upon this signed document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they stalled for time in honouring the disarmament agreement. That is why at the trials where I gave evidence, I got acquainted with documents Tolimir sent to the Main Staff in the context of exchanges, and I knew that the Muslim -- or, rather, he said that the Muslim side was dragging their feet --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please explain again what he said about exchanges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hasan Muratovic went to meet him at the airport and asked to be received by Slobodan Milosevic. He wanted that -- that armed brigade to cross the border to enter Serbia. And that was accepted. They were promised refugee status in Serbia, although they were armed. That's what I learned from Carl Bildt's book. So Tolimir's assessment was well founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. General, thank you very much. Thank you for answering our questions. And at this time, we have no questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. The interpreters in the previous answer said that they asked the witness to explain what he said about exchanges. Now, I don't know, Mr. Lukic, whether you were able to follow it in the original language and whether there's any need to ask the witness to do it still.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no any need -- need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need. Mr. McCloskey, any need for re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would hope 15 or 20 minutes and perhaps shorter, depending on the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, please proceed. And I leave it your hands whether it still makes sense, if you say possibly shorter, to ask the next witness to remain stand by, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: She's here. I think standby is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we start with P1785.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, just to -- this -- this is a Main Staff document to the president that was the subject of a discussion we had regarding standing in or whether it was Milovanovic's name on these when he was out in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could go to the last -- now that we see what this is, can we go to the last page. And we -- we see here clearly it's ... and -- well, if we could blow up the -- the one down, the Serbian. Where we can read the Serbian as something like "zastupa" and then we see clearly in the English, "standing in for the Chief of Staff" and it's Major-General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall whether this was the -- the basic layout of most of the -- such reports to the president during that time that General Milovanovic was in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It states here, "standing in for." Not for the Chief of Staff but standing in for the Chief of Staff, General -- Major-General Radivoje Miletic. After a certain period of time, while I was in the west, this started to appear. Probably due to the fact that General Milovanovic, in his communication with Miletic, asked him to put this. I've already said before this Tribunal that during a morning coffee, when a report like this arrived at the forward command post, General Jovo Maric was present. He was the chief of the air force and anti-aircraft administration. General Milovanovic said, "Excuse me, what is this Mico fucking with me?" When we looked at him, he said, "How can I write a report to myself?" And from that time on, this is what appears: Standing in for the Chief of Staff, Major-General Radivoje Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to P1087.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you talked about -- as part of any operation there should be a -- I think you called it a topographic map with an approval on it, and the author of the operation in the right-hand corner. I want to show you an original map that was obtained in a search of General Zivanovic's Serbian residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's page 25 in e-court. And we have -- if we could get some help, I think we've got an original that Ms. Stewart -- the Court may recall seeing this before when Mr. Ivetic and I were showing maps. If everybody could just take a look at it. And make sure that General Mladic sees it. And you're going to hurt the witness's neck if we can't -- well, I guess you're not there to change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, is this what you had in mind when you talked about a topographic map showing the approval?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a decision by the commander of the Drina Corps for active combat approved by the commander, Major-General, we have the title at the top, and then in the right-hand corner, it's signed by the person who drafted the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature of the commander of the Main Staff up in the left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's General Mladic's signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's go to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can get back that to Ms. Stewart. There's no other questions on that. If the -- thank you. That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, my notes say that on page 67 yesterday, lines 9 through 10, that you stated that whenever a new directive is issued, the previous directive is no longer in force. And you were talking about the time, Directive 7 and Directive 7/1. And I think the Defence would agree with me that Directive 7 is dated March 8th, 1995. The cover letter sending it to the corps was dated March 17th, 1995. And the date on Directive 7/1 is March 31st, 1995. So if we take you at your word, General, the Directive 7 would have only been in force for three weeks. That can't be right, can it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the situation at the front. Here, it's in force in that part where the auxiliary forces are being issued their assignments, that is the 1st Krajina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the Herzegovina Corps. That's where they are told that they are to act pursuant to the tasks issued in Directive 7/1. The main body of the force, in order to carry out the Sadejstvo operation, the 1st Krajina Corps, the Eastern Bosnia Corps, the Drina Corps, and the air force and anti-aircraft defence, they were given a different assignment, not the one that is stated in Directive 7. So the authors of the directive provided the assignments to one set of forces according to Directive 7, and the -- the tasks to the main body of the force is new in Directive 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I -- that does hopefully clear up a bit of that answer. I won't get into that in any more detail. And, lastly, we just saw a document and some questions from Mr. Lukic, I think there was a gazette, a law about the formation of a civilian body to control UN and humanitarian convoys. And I have an audio I want to play to you to see if you can comment on it. And -- but before I play that audio, were you -- were you aware that -- if General Mladic or perhaps the security folks at the Main Staff were ever taping their own communications between people and the outside, or with -- with -- inside the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is from an audiotape that was retrieved from the residence of General Mladic in one of those searches. It's 65 ter 1711A, and I have not dealt with this product before but we should have a transcript and I hope that it's hearable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not provided to the booth, the transcripts? I -- it has been. I -- I rely on the nodding of yes by Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Please let me -- let me just list it. It's fact number 9 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could for this first time perhaps ask the interpreters not to say anything so we can listen to it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we'll do is we play it first without translation -- translation of -- we see that there's also transcription on our screens. And perhaps if, during the second round, after the interpreters have had an opportunity to listen first, then to see whether we can receive translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That was -- that was one playing. Should we play it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please play it again and then we'll ... Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Low volume. Mr. Mladic, low volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you stopped at 1 minute, 30 [Realtime transcript read in error "0"] seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll play it again. Have the interpreters have had an opportunity to listen to it and was it sufficiently audible to do their job?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the tape is very, very inaudible, so if we read what we have, we cannot actually listen to the tape at the same time. So basically we would be reading from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then proceed on this basis, and if there's any comment on the accuracy of the -- of the English translation as transcribed, Mr. Lukic, we'd like to hear from you. Of course, not at this very moment but you have an opportunity to further verify the accuracy of translation and transcription.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The -- my remark was not properly recorded. I said you stopped at 1 minute, 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is hereby corrected. Could we play it again from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Please let me just list it. It's fact number 9. Then, mate, they again stopped the crossing over Nisici plateau in the direction of Visoko. And now when it started pounding on Sarajevo from the Nisici plateau, they did not send anyone to Srebrenica, to Zepa. They made a safe area for the Turks in Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, Bihac, Sarajevo, Tuzla. Not in the Muslim-controlled part of Sarajevo, nor in Capljina, nor in Mostar, nor in Zenica, nor in Tuzla. Although I asked for that, where we -- and they have become, damn it, a service of UNPROFOR and the international community. How many humanitarian aid convoys will come about which they argued with me for a year. And until I took everything, did not let anything through, I would not have taken Srebrenica or Zepa. If I had not starved them in the winter, since February I let them through only one or two convoys. But then, for example, at that time it didn't even cross their minds to come and see, except that Tomo Kovac came five days later, after the liberation of Srebrenica to look at the factory and if there was something he could steal from it, as he has been doing up to now. This is his only task. Among themselves -- you see first while there was in Pretis and when they had all looted all our factories with parts of the MUP Ministry of Interior of Serbia -- of individuals looted everybody."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do not believe that what we read actually corresponded to what is here. The sound quality was too poor for a faithful interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, under the circumstances I think we should work this out better. If you have any question in relation to what you think was said approximately, if you could phrase it in such a way that we are not relying directly on the text in this -- on this audio. It -- it seems, but correct me when I'm wrong, that at least there was comment by the person speaking on convoys, humanitarian convoys, and influence on those convoys over various periods of time. And I leave it to that at this moment. Could I -- I'm not asking the interpreters to confirm this, yes or no, but on the basis of such a suggestion, and it will turn out to be right or wrong, that has to be explored in further detail, you may put some questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I will get together with the Defence on this small portion. This has been very carefully gone over, as you need to do, obviously, with something like this, what cannot be done in a courtroom, and I am confident that it is accurate, but we'll work on that so you have better -- better information before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I know you've heard a lot of radio traffic in your time and that a -- your practiced ear. You recognised that voice, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised the voice of General Mladic. But I did not understand who he was addressing. And I could see that he was quite angry, outraged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you, in your time with General Mladic, know that he was angry that safe areas were not made for the areas that he -- he noted in this -- in this audio, that just, for whatever reason, the Muslims got the safe areas and the Serbs didn't?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can speak about specific things. I know that in the context -- in contacts it was not just that he was dissatisfied. We were all dissatisfied about the treatment of the sides to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you share some of the concerns that he was voicing in this -- in this short audio?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dissatisfaction was generally similar regarding the attitude or the position of the peacekeeping forces and other organisations from the UNHCR, the International Committee of the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders, because the situation in the area and the events demonstrated a certain partiality towards the other two sides, the Muslim and the Croatian side, in relation to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we were translated a comment that: But not for starving the enclaves, the VRS would not have taken them. Something to that degree. Can you tell us what you heard, if anything, on that topic? What you heard him say?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand what starving referred to. He was talking about Gorazde to Zepa, the protected enclaves. And he was mentioning -- or he was asking for protected zones or enclaves to be formed for the Serbian side, Mostar, Zenica. I don't know where else. I didn't understand this part. There was a lot of background noise in the headphones. And I don't know whom he was addressing, who he was talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, General. Thank you. That's, of course, not your job. So I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Lukic, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have to call that large map, it's P1087. And it's the map on Srebrenica action, operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have information that General Mladic signed this map on the 13th of July, 1995, but after the entire action was finished. Do you know anything about that? Do you know when General Mladic signed this map?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I seem to remember that he did that after the fact once the assignment from this order was executed, the order that was drafted by the Drina Corps. I don't know if it was Krstic or somebody else gave it to him to sign. I wasn't present but that is the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This would be all our questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no further questions for you, Mr. Obradovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, and whether by the parties or by the Judges, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have one request, if you permit me to greet General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not common to do that, but the mere fact that you've expressed the wish to do that may be sufficient. And he has heard that because that has been translated to Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, would you please remain to be seated. Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, your behaviour in this respect was inappropriate. We established that at this very moment it has no consequences but it is hereby on the record. We will adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 18th of July, at 9.30 in the morning, in Courtroom III.
